claims.claim: An experiment is a series of observations conducted under controlled conditions to study a relationship, with the purpose of drawing causal inferences about that relationship; it involves manipulation of an independent variable, measurement of a dependent variable, and exposure of participants to the conditions being studied.
In experiments, researchers actively make changes in one variable and watch for changes in another variable, and experiments are the method that allows researchers to make causal inferences.
The only way a researcher can claim that a relationship between variables is cause and effect is to perform an experiment; observing a relationship alone does not establish causation.

The independent variable is the variable in an experiment that is specifically manipulated in order to assess its effect; the dependent variable is the outcome observed to occur or change after variation of the independent variable.
A control variable is a variable that could affect the measured outcome but is not of particular interest to the researcher; it may be held at a constant level during the study to remove its effects.

The experimental group is the group of participants exposed to a particular manipulation of the independent variable; the control group is the comparison group whose members receive no intervention or an established intervention, and the responses of the two are compared.

Random assignment places participants in the conditions of an experiment entirely at random, giving each participant an equal likelihood of any condition; it makes the treatment and control groups approximately comparable in all respects except the treatment, which is why a difference at the end can be attributed to the manipulation.

Experiments are often conducted in very artificial settings, which calls into question how well the findings apply to real-world settings, and many questions psychologists would like to answer cannot be pursued experimentally (for example, for ethical reasons).

conflictingEvidence.issue: Framing of random selection versus random assignment
positions: The APA Dictionary's experiment entry states that random selection of participants and their random assignment to conditions are both necessary in experiments.

The Noba Research Designs module presents random assignment (deciding which condition each participant enters by chance) as the critical feature that makes groups comparable, without discussing random selection.
Sampling/random selection is the property of the research-methods sibling topic.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson follows the APA definition for the working definition of an experiment and teaches random assignment as the core group-formation step, which is this topic's scope; random selection is left to the research-methods sibling topic. No factual conflict among sources.
